title: ER Cardinality, Mapping, and Weak Entities
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs test whether candidates can map ER cardinality to tables correctly and reason about participation and weak entities.

phases.goal: Establish cardinality ratios, descriptive attributes, and weak-entity identity.

must_hit.point: Cardinality (degree of relationship) is the number of entity instances that can associate across a relationship.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States cardinality as how many instances of one entity set can link to instances of another via a relationship.

must_hit.point: The four primary cardinality ratios are 1:1, 1:M, M:1, and M:N (M-M).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all four ratios by name without inventing extra types.

must_hit.point: A descriptive attribute sits on the relationship diamond and records a property of the association, not of either entity alone.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives an example like Date on an order-placement relationship belonging to the association event.

must_hit.point: A weak entity has no primary key of its own and depends on an owner (strong) entity for identification.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines weak entity via missing independent key and existence dependency on an owner.

probes: What is cardinality in an ER model, and what are the four primary cardinality ratios?
What makes an entity weak, and how is a partial key different from a primary key?

hints.1: Think about allowable connections between two entity sets, then about entities that cannot stand alone.
hints.2: Name the four ratios; for weak entities mention owner, total participation, and discriminator.
hints.3: Cardinality = how many instances associate; ratios are 1:1, 1:M, M:1, M:N; weak entity has no own PK and uses a partial key within one owner.

phases.goal: Show how cardinality drives foreign-key placement, table absorption, and weak-entity table keys.

must_hit.point: Golden rule: foreign-key placement and whether a relationship becomes its own table depend entirely on cardinality, aiming to reduce tables when sound.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties mapping decisions to cardinality and the goal of fewer tables without losing information.

must_hit.point: For 1:1, combine into one table (or keep two and put the other's key as a foreign key on either side); if merged, the primary key can be either side's key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions merge flexibility and that either entity's key can be the merged PK.

must_hit.point: For 1:M, put the foreign key (PK of the 1 side) on the many side and absorb the relationship table; descriptive attributes migrate with that FK.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says FK goes on many, relationship is absorbed, and attributes like Date land on the many-side table.

must_hit.point: For M:N, create a separate junction table holding both keys with composite PK of both keys; M:N cannot be absorbed into either side.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Insists on a relationship table with composite {both keys} and no reduction.

must_hit.point: A mapped weak-entity table is owner PK plus partial key plus its own attributes, with composite PK {owner PK, partial key}.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives form like Dependent(EID, Name, age) with composite PK of owner key and Name.

probes: How do you map 1:1, 1:M, and M:N relationships to relations?
How do you turn a weak entity into a table?

hints.1: Ask where the foreign key lives for each cardinality before counting tables.
hints.2: 1:1 can merge; 1:M puts FK on many and absorbs; M:N needs a junction; weak = owner key + partial key.
hints.3: State the three mapping rules plus weak-entity composite PK = {owner PK, partial key}.

phases.goal: Contrast when relationships can be absorbed to cut tables versus when a separate table is mandatory.

must_hit.point: 1:1 offers maximal flexibility: merging often reduces table count; alternatively keep two tables with a FK on either side.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains merge-to-one versus two-table-with-FK as valid 1:1 choices aimed at fewer tables.

must_hit.point: 1:M absorbs the relationship into the many side to reduce overall tables; M:N cannot reduce and must keep a separate relationship table.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts absorption for 1:M with mandatory junction for M:N to avoid redundancy.

probes: When can you absorb a relationship into an entity table, and when must you keep a separate relationship table?
Why does absorbing an M:N relationship fail even though absorbing 1:M succeeds?

hints.1: Compare what happens if you put both keys only inside one participating entity table.
hints.2: Link absorption to 1-side FK on many versus needing both keys as a composite relationship PK.
hints.3: 1:M absorbs into many; M:N needs a junction—absorbing M:N causes redundancy and insert anomalies.

phases.goal: Apply mapping reductions and total-participation cardinality reasoning to exam-style questions.

must_hit.point: In the minimum-tables ER model, the answer is 3 tables: strong entity alone, 1:M folded with its many side, and M:N as its own table.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says (b) 3 with T1=strong entity, T2=1:M·many side, T3=M:N relationship.

must_hit.point: For a many-to-one R from E1 to E2 with total participation of both and |E1| greater than |E2|, every entity in E1 is associated with exactly one entity in E2.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Selects GATE option (A) and rejects claims that some E1 maps to multiple E2 or that each E2 has exactly/at most one E1.

probes: Given an ER diagram with a 1:M and an M:N among strong entities, what is the minimum number of tables and why?
If R is many-to-one from E1 to E2 with total participation and |E1| > |E2|, which statement about R must be true?

hints.1: Count one table per strong entity that cannot fold, then add what M:N forces.
hints.2: Many-to-one from E1 to E2 means each E1 points to one E2; |E1| > |E2| forces some E2 to have several E1.
hints.3: Minimum tables answer is 3; GATE answer is every E1 associates with exactly one E2.

tradeoffs.topic: Merge 1:1 into one table vs keep two tables with a foreign key
tradeoffs.strong_answer: 1:1 allows either merge (PK can be either side's key) or two tables with the other's key as FK on either side; merging is preferred when the goal is minimizing tables without losing information.

tradeoffs.topic: Absorb relationship (1:M) vs separate junction table (M:N)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: 1:M puts the 1-side PK as FK on the many side and absorbs the relationship (and descriptive attributes) into that table; M:N must create a junction with composite PK of both keys because absorbing into either side causes redundancy and insert anomalies.

gotchas.trap: Absorbing an M:N relationship into either participating table to reduce table count
gotchas.correction: M:N cannot reduce; you must create a separate relationship table with composite primary key of both keys—absorbing causes massive redundancy and insert anomalies.

gotchas.trap: Treating a weak entity as having its own standalone primary key
gotchas.correction: A weak entity has no PK of its own; identification uses owner PK plus partial key (discriminator), with total participation in the identifying relationship.

gotchas.trap: From many-to-one E1→E2 with |E1| > |E2| and total participation, concluding each E2 has exactly one or at most one E1
gotchas.correction: Each E1 maps to exactly one E2, but |E1| > |E2| forces some E2 entities to associate with several E1 entities, so those E2-side uniqueness claims are false.
